## Legitimacy and public support

-   what are the determinants of public support for courts?

-   to what extent are courts immune from changes in public opinion?

-   this week: why and how public support matters for courts, what it is made of, how courts cultivate it and how we measure it

# Why support matters for courts

## Public support as a source of judicial power {.smaller}

-   the US Supreme Court's power over the executive depends on **the public** being aware of the case [@carrubba2010executive]

-   in democracies, people generally hold courts in high regard [@vanberg2015constitutional]

    -   the US Supreme Court followed long-term trends in public opinion until the early 1980s [@mishler1993supreme]

-   attacking courts or ignoring their rulings can be politically costly [@vanberg2015constitutional]

## Trust across institutions {.smaller}

-   across 33 OECD countries in late 2025, 54% reported high or moderately high trust in the courts and judicial system, against 40% for the national government [@oecd2026oecd]

    -   Denmark: 77% for the courts, 44% for the government

-   the same ordering holds in Britain: in a 2026 British Election Study sample, the Supreme Court was the most trusted of six institutions and political parties the least [@ovadek2026contagion]

-   in 30 of 33 OECD countries, courts are trusted more than parliament and government [@oecd2026oecd]

## Is trust in courts its own thing? {.smaller}

-   trust in parliaments and in courts tends to move together [@oecd2024oecd], which has two readings

    -   **elite contagion**: one governing establishment, so distrust of one branch spreads to the others

    -   **institutional substitution**: checks and balances, so distrust of one branch raises trust in the branch that constrains it

-   a British Election Study experiment on Parliament, the UK Supreme Court and the ECtHR [@ovadek2026contagion]

    -   an unpopular parliamentary decision lowered trust in the courts more than in Parliament

    -   an unpopular ruling lowered trust in that court and others, not in Parliament

    -   popular decisions, party cues and information on judges' conduct did not move trust

-   the reservoir of goodwill can be drained by decisions the courts never made

## Support as a shield {.smaller}

-   public support makes enforcement more likely and makes legislators wary of open defiance [@vanberg2001legislativejudicial]

-   does support deter court curbing?

    -   in experiments, US voters punish incumbents who attack courts, and court supporters punish most [@driscoll2023costs]

    -   co-partisans punish less, and party and issue positions matter more

    -   but Americans back curbing the Supreme Court when they disagree with its rulings [@bartels2020curbing]

    -   Germans with populist attitudes would curb the constitutional court like any other institution [@peffley2024populism]

    -   the shield holds only where the public values the institution over the outcome

## Courts track public opinion {.smaller}

-   if support is a resource, courts should protect it, and the evidence suggests they do

    -   the US Supreme Court's decisions move with public mood over time [@mishler1993supreme; @casillas2011how]

    -   the US Supreme Court is most constrained by outside pressure when others must implement its rulings [@hall2014semiconstrained]

    -   unpopular courts behave differently when the public is paying attention [@krehbiel2021public]

-   a court that tracks opinion may keep its support but gives up the counter-majoritarian role that justified it

## Maintaining public support {.smaller}

-   to maintain diffuse support, it is arguably in courts' long-term interests to stay ideologically **close to the median** voter

-   courts can offer compensation to the "losers" to increase acceptance [@gonzalezocantos2019compensation]

-   courts might care less about maintaining public support when

    -   they are aligned with the executive (for enforcement)

    -   the public is not paying attention (but see @casillas2011how)

    -   public opinion is less important (autocracies)

# What support is made of

## Legitimacy

> Legitimacy is a psychological property of an authority, institution, or social arrangement that leads those connected to it to believe that it is appropriate, proper, and just. [@tyler2006psychological]

-   sometimes used interchangeably with "authority" and "diffuse support"

    -   conceptually different from "specific support" (but measurement difficulties)

## Judicial legitimacy

-   unlike democratic parliaments and executives, most courts cannot derive their legitimacy from electoral mandates

-   at the same time, courts rely on diffuse support for effectiveness more than other branches

-   particularly important when constituents disagree over a policy decision [@gibson2014losing]

## Sources of judicial legitimacy {.smaller}

-   traditionally, legalism and **legal symbols** are seen as the main source of legitimacy, as in positivity theory [@gibson2014losing; @gibson2017reconsidering]

    -   symbols make courts seem fairer and **different from politics**

    -   awareness means more exposure to symbols and a "reservoir of goodwill"

    -   but in Norway and Portugal, partisan framing of a ruling lowers acceptance while policy framing does not [@magalhaes2023beyond]

-   on the rival **ideological** account, Americans ascribe less legitimacy to the Supreme Court when they think they disagree with it [@bartels2013ideological]

## Where does support come from? {.smaller}

| source of support | claim |
|----------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| legal symbols | exposure to courts builds a reservoir of goodwill |
| ideological agreement | people support courts they agree with, as after *Dobbs* [@gibson2024losing] |
| partisan alignment | in Argentina, trust in courts fell among government supporters after rulings checked the government [@gandur2025trust] |
| institutional quality | in Europe, independent and accountable judiciaries are trusted more [@garoupa2021public] |
| awareness | to know courts is to love them, or not [@levendusky2024has] |
| democratic values | commitment to democracy supports independent courts, or not |
| identity cues | judges' identities signal fairness |

## Political foundations {.smaller}

-   we would expect that individuals holding **democratic values** are more supportive of judicial independence [@caldeira1992etiology]

    -   @bartels2023can find no evidence that democratic values softened partisan backlash after Kenya's 2017 election rulings

    -   @cheruvu2025partisanship find that Hungarian opposition voters' support for backlash against the CJEU depends on their commitment to democracy

-   a study of 34 African countries shows that presidential **co-partisanship decreases support** for horizontal judicial power and increases it for vertical [@bartels2020does]

    -   support for courts depends on who is in power

## Political context {.smaller}

-   in line with positivity theory, greater **awareness** of a court should be associated with more support for its independence [@gibson2014losing]

-   @gandur2025awareness show that this relationship is affected by the political context

    -   in Poland and Hungary, perceived **executive influence**, not awareness, goes with demand for judicial independence

    -   @demicheli2024public similarly find that more educated Latin Americans trust courts more only where institutions are strong

-   identification with the AfD lowers trust in Germany's Federal Constitutional Court [@arzheimer2025identification]

-   illiberal views about justice go with lower trust in the EU, the ECtHR and national courts [@voeten2022is]

## Anti-system parties

![Trust in the Federal Constitutional Court among AfD identifiers and others, 2013–2017 [@arzheimer2025identification]](img/afd-trust-fcc.jpg)

## Perceptions of judicial fairness {.smaller}

-   judges' identity categories operate as ideological cues affecting perceptions of judicial fairness [@bracic2023because]

    -   marginalized identities increase Democrats' perceptions of fairness, impartiality and trust in SCOTUS

    -   Republicans see gay judges as less fair and impartial than straight judges

-   the public does not seek descriptive representation as such [@bracic2023because]

    -   people prefer judges who (they assume) will think like them, not just look like them

## Descriptive representation and trust {.smaller}

-   does a bench that looks like the public earn more trust from it?

-   Black respondents rated the US federal courts as more legitimate when told about Black judges, and white respondents as less legitimate [@scherer2010does]

-   @moyer2026does finds women on the federal bench raise trust only slightly, briefly and among Democrats

-   race representation splits Black and white respondents, while gender representation barely moves trust

## International courts and public opinion

-   support for international courts is context dependent

    -   evidence that complementarity arguments raise support for the ICC is modest and varies by country [@zvobgo2025complementarity]

-   but public confidence in the ICC goes with confidence in national courts and the UN [@stappert2025between]

::: notes
Zvobgo and Chaudoin (2025) find only modest evidence that complementarity arguments raise support for the ICC in five countries
:::

## Measuring legitimacy {.smaller}

-   **diffuse support** (legitimacy) is loyalty to the institution regardless of what it does, while **specific support** is approval of its recent decisions

-   the standard battery asks about abolishing the court, curbing its jurisdiction, trusting it and its involvement in politics [@gibson2003measuring]

-   most cross-national surveys have a single item, "trust in the courts", which critics say mixes the two [@gibson2003measuring]

-   @hemrajani2026trust finds the trust item is a valid and comparable measure of legitimacy

-   cross-national comparison needs the same questions asked at the same time; smoothing across surveys is one workaround [@claassen2019estimating]

## Trust in courts, over time and across countries {.smaller}

-   <https://trustincourts.netlify.app/>: an annual trust estimate for each country, with its uncertainty

-   built by harmonizing surveys that ask different questions on different scales in different years, using a measurement model

-   compare countries, follow one country over time, and set trust in courts against trust in the national parliament

-   a starting point for a research paper on why trust differs between countries or moves within one

# How courts reach the public

## How courts reach the public {.smaller}

-   what the public knows of courts mostly arrives through the media, and courts manage that

-   Germany's Federal Constitutional Court issues press releases more often for rulings that change the status quo [@meyer2020judicial]

-   the Mexican Supreme Court promoted its rulings to the press selectively, believing this would build its authority [@staton2006constitutional]

-   the UK Supreme Court streams its hearings and hands down judgments on camera; the US Supreme Court still refuses cameras

-   being elected adds to US state courts' legitimacy, while campaign contributions reduce it and attack ads matter little [@gibson2012electing]

-   many Americans cannot name a Supreme Court justice, though recall questions understate what they know [@gibson2009knowing]

# Rulings that land mid-survey

## Rulings that land mid-survey {.smaller}

-   surveys take weeks to field, and if a ruling drops in the middle, respondents interviewed before and after can be compared as if randomly assigned

    -   the **unexpected event during survey design** [@munoz2020unexpected]

-   the design assumes the ruling was unexpected, interview timing is as good as random and nothing else changed

-   applied to Argentine rulings by @gandur2025trust

-   checks ask whether the before and after samples are alike and whether opinion was already trending
